chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ja'far ibn al-Muthanna al-Khatib, from Muhammad ibn al-Fudayl and Bishr ibn Ismail, who said:

Muhammad ibn Ismail said to me: 'Shall I cheer you up, O son of Muthanna?' I said: 'Yes,' and I arose to him. He said: 'This indecent man entered just now, so he sat opposite Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him). Then he turned to him and said to him: 'O Abu al-Hasan, what do you say regarding the one in Ihram, can he shade himself on the carriage?' He said to him: 'No.' He said: 'So can he shade himself in the tent?' He said to him: 'Yes.' So he repeated the words to him, like a scoffer, laughing, saying: 'O Abu al-Hasan, so what is the difference between this and this?' He said: 'O Abu Yusuf, indeed the Religion is not by analogy, like your analogies. You are playing with the Religion. We did as the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) did, and we said as the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said. The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) used to ride his mount, so he did not shade himself upon it, and the sun bothered him, so he would cover part of his body with the other part, and sometimes he would cover his face with his hand. And when he dismounted, he would shade himself in the tent, and in the house, and by the wall.'
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on shading from the sun for a person in Ihram according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith, narrated by Ja'far al-Sadiq (AS), highlights the Shia jurisprudential principle of 'La ad-dina bi-qiyas' (religion is not based on analogical reasoning), contrasting it with the Sunni reliance on Qiyas. It establishes that the permissibility of shading for the Muhrim is derived strictly from the Sunnah of the Prophet (PBUH), who covered his body while riding and used tents or walls when stationary, rather than applying logical deduction. This underscores the Shia emphasis on textual precedent over rational analogy in deriving legal rulings.
